title: it's fine
subtitle: when two small words do a lot of work

steps.text: this one's about two small words you probably said today.

steps.scene: your friend cancels an hour before. you'd been looking forward to it all week. you text back: "no worries, it's fine!"
steps.reveal: the text took four words. the evening felt a lot longer.
steps.prompt: ever sent a text like that?

steps.scene: someone asks how your week was. it was a lot. you hear yourself say, "it's fine, just busy."
steps.reveal: underneath "fine" there might have been: tired. a little alone. proud you got through it.

steps.scene: your coffee comes out different from what you ordered. "it's fine," you say, and drink it.
steps.reveal: sometimes it really is fine. and sometimes "fine" is just quicker than wanting something.

lines: "it's fine" isn't a lie. it's a shortcut.
it ends the moment quickly, keeps things smooth, and keeps you out of the way. if speaking up ever caused trouble for you, of course you got good at it.
the cost is quiet. the more often "fine" speaks for you, the harder it gets to know what you actually feel, or want.

steps.prompt: which one would you want to send?

options.note: smooth for them. the disappointment stays with you.

options.text: aw, i was really looking forward to it. rain check?
options.note: honest and still kind. they get to know you a little.
the feeling gets out, just sideways.

steps.footer: all three make sense. you get to choose.

steps.context: someone safe asks how your week was.
steps.prompt: what would feel true to say?

options.note: quick, and the conversation moves on.

options.text: honestly, kind of a lot. but i got through it.
options.note: true, and it gives them a way in.

options.text: long. i'll tell you about it sometime.
options.note: honest without telling everything. you decide how much to share.

steps.context: after a hard day, alone, you tell yourself:
steps.original: it's fine. other people have it worse.
steps.prompt: what if you said it a notch kinder?

options.text: it's fine. other people have it worse.
options.note: it skips past your day without looking at it.

options.text: today was hard. that's allowed, even if others have it harder.
i'm tired. i think i could use some rest.
options.note: names it, then asks what you need.

steps.context: the coffee that came out different.
steps.prompt: how would you like to handle it?

options.note: sometimes it truly is. that's okay too.

options.text: sorry, i think i ordered an oat latte?
options.note: a small want, said out loud. it usually goes better than we expect.

options.text: it's fine. next time i'll say something.

steps.prompt: think of one "fine" from this week. what might have been underneath it?

input.label: i could have said:
input.placeholder: e.g. actually, i'd rather stay in tonight

steps.prompt: want to keep any of these for later?
phrases: i'm a little bummed, but it's okay.
it's not a big deal, but it does matter to me.
can i get back to you on that?

steps.prompt: one small thing for today, if you want:
options: next time you hear yourself say "it's fine," just notice it. no need to change anything.
swap one "it's fine" for one honest word, like "tired" or "bummed."
say one small preference out loud, like what you'd rather eat or watch.

steps.text: that's it. you don't have to stop saying "fine." you just get to choose when it's true.

grounding.idea: putting feelings into words can lower their intensity
telling feelings apart is linked to healthier coping and can be practiced
grounding.source: Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight, 2015, Current Directions in Psychological Science

grounding.idea: honest, respectful expression of needs and preferences (assertive communication) is a standard skill in cognitive behavioral approaches
